question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, on what basis may the Commission investigate an applicant or licensee?
choice_a: Upon its own motion, or upon the sworn written request of any person alleging a violation
choice_b: Only upon a court order compelling investigation
choice_c: Only after a criminal conviction has already occurred
choice_d: Only upon request of another state's licensing authority
explanation: The Commission may investigate the actions of any applicant or licensee upon its own motion, and shall investigate upon the sworn written request of any person alleging a violation of the chapter or its rules.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, within what period must an investigation generally be commenced, absent an exception?
choice_a: Within three years of the act giving rise to the investigation
choice_b: Within six months of the act
choice_c: Within one year of the act
choice_d: There is no time limit under any circumstance
explanation: Except for investigations of applicants or cases involving fraud or pending court litigation, the Commission generally may not commence an investigation more than three years after the conduct at issue.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, which two categories of matters are exempted from the general three-year limit on commencing an investigation?
choice_a: Investigations of applicants, and cases involving fraud or pending court litigation
choice_b: Investigations involving fewer than three affiliated licensees
choice_c: Investigations initiated by a competitor broker
choice_d: Investigations of firms with fewer than five employees
explanation: The three-year limitation on commencing an investigation does not apply to investigations of applicants or to cases involving fraud or pending court litigation.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, what enforcement mechanism is available if a person refuses to comply with a Commission subpoena issued during an investigation?
choice_a: The Commission or commissioner may seek an order from superior court compelling compliance
choice_b: The subpoena automatically becomes void after 10 days
choice_c: The Commission must refer the matter to the Attorney General for criminal prosecution
choice_d: No enforcement mechanism exists; compliance is voluntary
explanation: The commissioner or chairperson may issue subpoenas to compel production of writings, documents, or material during an authorized investigation, and superior court enforcement is available if a subpoena is not obeyed.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, what is the general rule regarding disclosure of an investigative record maintained by the Commission?
choice_a: It may not be released for any purpose other than a hearing, review by another lawful licensing/law enforcement authority upon subpoena, or at the Commission's discretion by majority vote of a quorum
choice_b: It must be posted publicly online within 10 days of closing the file
choice_c: It may be released to any member of the public upon written request
choice_d: It may only ever be released to the licensee under investigation
explanation: Investigative records are confidential; release is limited to use in a hearing, review by another law enforcement agency or lawful licensing authority upon subpoena, or at the Commission's discretion upon an affirmative vote of a majority of a quorum.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, can an investigative record maintained by the Commission be subpoenaed in a civil action between private parties?
choice_a: No -- investigative records are protected from subpoena in civil litigation
choice_b: Yes, any party to civil litigation may subpoena the full file
choice_c: Only if both parties to the civil action consent
choice_d: Only after the investigation has been closed for at least five years
explanation: No part of an investigative record maintained by the Commission may be subpoenaed for use in a civil action, protecting the confidentiality of the investigative process.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, what may the Commission do after revoking or suspending a licensee's license?
choice_a: Publish the name of that licensee, such as on the Commission's website or in official publications
choice_b: Nothing; publication of a licensee's name is prohibited under all circumstances
choice_c: It must obtain the licensee's written consent before any publication
choice_d: It may only publish the licensee's name in a printed newspaper of general circulation
explanation: Upon revocation or suspension of a license, the Commission may publish the name of the licensee, such as through its website or official publications.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-27, for which categories of Commission activity may the public be excluded from a meeting?
choice_a: Disciplinary deliberations, settlement negotiations, and review of the results of investigations
choice_b: All Commission meetings of every kind, without exception
choice_c: Only meetings concerning fee schedules
choice_d: Only meetings where fewer than three commissioners are present
explanation: The Commission may close a meeting to the public during disciplinary deliberations, settlement negotiations, and review of the results of investigations, consistent with the confidentiality protections built into the investigative process.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, how are citations and letters of findings characterized under the chapter?
choice_a: They are not construed as a disciplinary sanction
choice_b: They are treated identically to a full license revocation
choice_c: They automatically convert into a formal sanction after one year
choice_d: They may only be issued by the Attorney General, not the Commission
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2 provides the Commission with alternatives to standard sanctions, expressly stating that citations and letters of findings are not to be construed as a disciplinary sanction.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, what is the maximum fine the Commission may impose per violation via citation, and the maximum total for multiple violations in one citation?
choice_a: $1,000 per violation, capped at $5,000 in any one citation
choice_b: $500 per violation, with no aggregate cap
choice_c: $10,000 per violation, capped at $50,000
choice_d: There is no dollar cap; the Commission sets fines case by case
explanation: A citation may include a fine of up to $1,000 for each violation, with fines for multiple violations limited to a total of $5,000 in any one citation.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, what happens if a licensee who receives a citation does not request a hearing within the allotted time?
choice_a: The licensee has 30 days to request a hearing; if none is requested, the citation order becomes final
choice_b: The citation is automatically voided after 30 days
choice_c: The licensee has one year to request a hearing
choice_d: A hearing is scheduled automatically regardless of whether one is requested
explanation: A citation must provide the recipient 30 days within which to request a hearing; if no hearing is requested within that window, the citation order becomes final.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-25.2, under what circumstance may the Commission issue a letter of findings instead of a citation or formal sanction, and what protection applies to it?
choice_a: When the violation appears to have caused no harm to a third party or the public; the letter remains confidential, is excluded from the licensee's public history, and cannot be subpoenaed in a civil proceeding
choice_b: Only for first-time salesperson licensees, and it is posted publicly
choice_c: Only when the licensee requests it in writing, and it is always subject to subpoena
choice_d: Only for firm-level violations, never for individual licensees
explanation: A letter of findings may be issued where the violation appears to have caused no harm to a third party or the public; it remains confidential, is excluded from the licensee's public license history, and cannot be subpoenaed in a civil proceeding.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-16(a), what happens when the Commission denies a properly filed application accompanied by the appropriate fees?
choice_a: The Commission must provide an opportunity for a hearing in accordance with the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act
choice_b: The applicant has no further recourse and must reapply from scratch
choice_c: The denial is automatically referred to a jury trial
choice_d: The applicant may only appeal directly to the Georgia Supreme Court
explanation: Where the Commission denies a properly filed application accompanied by the appropriate fees, it must provide the applicant an opportunity for a hearing in accordance with Chapter 13 of Title 50, the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-16(b), once an applicant has exhausted administrative remedies and received an unfavorable final decision on a denied application, where must initial judicial review be sought?
choice_a: Solely in the superior court of the county in which the Commission is domiciled, overriding the standard venue provisions of the Georgia APA
choice_b: In any superior court of the applicant's choosing statewide
choice_c: In the Georgia Court of Appeals as a court of first instance
choice_d: In the county where the applicant currently resides, regardless of the Commission's location
explanation: Initial judicial review of a final Commission decision on a denied application is available solely in the superior court of the county in which the Commission is domiciled, a specific exception to the general venue rules of the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-26(a), before the Commission may censure a licensee or revoke/suspend a license, what must it provide?
choice_a: An opportunity for a hearing under the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act
choice_b: A public referendum on the licensee's conduct
choice_c: A private mediation session with no right to a hearing
choice_d: Nothing; the Commission may act unilaterally with no process
explanation: Before censuring a licensee or revoking or suspending a license, the Commission must provide an opportunity for a hearing consistent with the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-26(b), what happens if a licensee or applicant fails to appear at a disciplinary hearing after being properly served notice?
choice_a: The proceeding may continue in the licensee's or applicant's absence
choice_b: The case is automatically dismissed
choice_c: The hearing must be postponed indefinitely until the licensee appears
choice_d: The Commission must file criminal charges for nonappearance
explanation: If a licensee or applicant fails to appear at a hearing after being properly served with notice, the proceeding may continue in their absence.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-26(b), if a licensee or applicant cannot be located or reached for service of Commission documents, who is deemed to be their agent for that purpose?
choice_a: The real estate commissioner
choice_b: The licensee's most recent qualifying broker, automatically
choice_c: The clerk of the Fulton County Superior Court
choice_d: No one; service is simply excused entirely
explanation: Where a licensee or applicant cannot be reached, the real estate commissioner is deemed to be their agent for purposes of service of Commission documents.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-10(2), what must a firm authorize its qualifying broker to do with respect to a contested case?
choice_a: Bind the firm to any settlement of a contested case before the Commission in which the firm is a named respondent
choice_b: Personally pay any fine assessed against affiliated licensees out of pocket
choice_c: Waive the firm's right to any hearing whatsoever
choice_d: Appoint outside counsel without informing the firm's owners
explanation: A firm seeking a broker's license must authorize its qualifying broker to bind the firm to any settlement of a contested case before the Commission, as defined under the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act, in which the firm is a named respondent.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-18(a), what must a licensee who operates at multiple business locations comply with?
choice_a: All local business ordinances affecting the licensee's business operations at each location
choice_b: Only the ordinances of the location where the qualifying broker resides
choice_c: Only state law; local ordinances never apply to licensed real estate firms
choice_d: Only the ordinances in effect at the time the firm was first licensed
explanation: A licensee conducting business from multiple locations must comply with all local business ordinances affecting operations at each of those locations.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-18(b), a broker may avoid vicarious liability for an affiliated licensee's violation by showing which three things?
choice_a: Reasonable supervisory procedures existed, and the broker did not participate in or ratify the violation
choice_b: The broker was on vacation at the time, had no knowledge of the firm's existence, and never met the licensee
choice_c: The affiliated licensee was terminated within 24 hours of discovery, with no other showing required
choice_d: The firm carried general liability insurance covering the violation
explanation: A broker may be shielded from vicarious liability for an affiliated licensee's violation by demonstrating that reasonable supervisory procedures were in place, and that the broker did not participate in or ratify the violation.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-18(d), if a broker delegates a supervisory duty to another person within the firm, what remains true?
choice_a: The broker or qualifying broker remains responsible for the acts of the person to whom the duty was delegated
choice_b: The broker is entirely relieved of responsibility once the duty is delegated
choice_c: Delegation is prohibited under all circumstances
choice_d: Responsibility shifts entirely and permanently to the delegate, even after the delegate leaves the firm
explanation: Delegation of a supervisory duty does not eliminate the broker's or qualifying broker's ultimate responsibility; they remain responsible for the acts of the person to whom the duty was delegated.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-18(e), what authority must a qualifying broker have regardless of whether the firm is organized as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, or limited partnership?
choice_a: Signatory authority over the firm's trust or escrow accounts
choice_b: Majority voting control of the firm's board of directors
choice_c: Sole ownership of at least 51% of the firm's equity
choice_d: Personal liability insurance in an amount set by the Secretary of State
explanation: Regardless of the firm's business entity type, the qualifying broker must have signatory authority over the firm's trust accounts, ensuring accountability for client funds.

question: Per Rule 520-1-.07, when a firm advertises specific properties for sale using a trade name or as a franchisee, what must appear in that advertising?
choice_a: The firm's name as registered with the Commission, clearly and unmistakably identifying the firm responsible for the listing
choice_b: Only the trade name, with no reference to the underlying registered firm name
choice_c: The individual licensee's personal name only, without any firm identification
choice_d: No firm identification is required if a trade name is used
explanation: Under Rule 520-1-.07, a firm using a trade name or franchise name must clearly and unmistakably include its Commission-registered firm name in advertising specific properties, so the public can identify the responsible firm.

question: Under Rule 520-1-.07, if a corporation wishes to conduct business under a trade name, what must it submit to the Commission?
choice_a: A certified copy of the trade name, certified by the County Clerk
choice_b: A notarized affidavit signed by every affiliated licensee
choice_c: Nothing; corporations are exempt from trade name registration
choice_d: Proof of federal trademark registration only
explanation: A corporation seeking to conduct business under a trade name must submit a certified copy of the trade name, certified by the County Clerk, and the trade name is then reflected on the broker's certificate of licensure.

question: Per Rule 520-1-.07, if a partnership, LLC, or corporation's qualifying broker ceases to serve in that role, what must the firm do within 60 days?
choice_a: Secure a new qualifying broker, or cease all real estate brokerage activity until it does
choice_b: Dissolve the firm entirely and refund all client deposits
choice_c: Notify only its affiliated licensees; no Commission action is required
choice_d: Automatically transfer its license to the departing broker's new firm
explanation: When a firm's qualifying broker ceases to serve, the firm has 60 days to secure a replacement qualifying broker or it must cease all real estate brokerage activity until it does so.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-11, where must the license of an affiliated licensee (such as a salesperson) be kept?
choice_a: In the custody and control of the real estate broker for whom the licensee acts
choice_b: In the licensee's personal home safe
choice_c: On permanent file at the Georgia Secretary of State's office only
choice_d: Mailed directly to the client at the start of every transaction
explanation: The license of each affiliated licensee is delivered or mailed to the broker for whom the licensee acts and must be kept in that broker's custody and control.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-11, what does the Commission issue to licensees to serve as portable proof of active licensure?
choice_a: A pocket identification card
choice_b: A laminated wall certificate only, with no portable equivalent
choice_c: A state-issued driver's license endorsement
choice_d: A digital-only QR code with no physical card option ever provided
explanation: The Commission provides licensees with a pocket identification card that serves as portable verification that the holder has an active real estate license.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(a), nonresidents who held a valid Georgia real estate license before what date retain licensure eligibility without meeting the chapter's newer nonresident requirements?
choice_a: July 1, 1991
choice_b: January 1, 1985
choice_c: July 1, 2000
choice_d: January 1, 1975
explanation: Nonresidents who held a Georgia license before July 1, 1991 remain eligible without meeting the newer nonresident requirements, unless they let that license lapse or apply for a different license type.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(a), what causes a grandfathered pre-1991 nonresident licensee to lose the benefit of that grandfathered status?
choice_a: Allowing the license to lapse, or applying for a different type of license
choice_b: Simply renewing the same license on time, which automatically ends grandfathered status
choice_c: Moving to a different address within the same home state
choice_d: Nothing can ever cause loss of grandfathered status
explanation: A nonresident's pre-July 1, 1991 grandfathered eligibility ends if the nonresident allows that license to lapse or applies for a different type of license.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(c), a nonresident who IS currently licensed in another state must show proof of what to obtain a Georgia license?
choice_a: Current, satisfactory licensure in the applicant's state of residence
choice_b: Five years of unlicensed practical experience
choice_c: A graduate degree in business administration
choice_d: Ownership of real property located in Georgia
explanation: A nonresident already licensed elsewhere must show satisfactory proof of current licensure in their state of residence as part of the Georgia licensure requirements.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(c), a nonresident applicant licensed elsewhere must sign a statement agreeing to what?
choice_a: That the applicant has read this chapter and its rules and agrees to abide by them in all Georgia brokerage activity
choice_b: That the applicant waives all rights to a hearing on any future complaint
choice_c: That the applicant will relocate to Georgia within one year
choice_d: That the applicant will not compete with resident Georgia licensees
explanation: The nonresident applicant must sign a statement acknowledging they have read the chapter and its rules and regulations and agree to abide by them in all brokerage activity conducted in Georgia.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(c), an individual nonresident applicant seeking licensure as a community association manager, salesperson, or associate broker must do what as part of the application?
choice_a: Affiliate with a resident or nonresident broker
choice_b: Obtain sponsorship from a sitting Commission member
choice_c: Complete an additional 200 hours of coursework beyond resident requirements
choice_d: Post a $50,000 surety bond with the Commission
explanation: An individual nonresident applicant for a CAM, salesperson, or associate broker license must affiliate with a broker who is either a Georgia resident or a licensed nonresident broker.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(c), a nonresident applicant licensed in another state must provide the Commission with what regarding their history in that state?
choice_a: Their disciplinary records from that other state
choice_b: A notarized personal reference letter from a local Georgia resident
choice_c: Their federal tax returns for the past three years
choice_d: A copy of their college diploma, regardless of relevance to real estate
explanation: As part of the nonresident licensure requirements, the applicant must provide the Commission with disciplinary records from the state in which they hold licensure.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(c), for purposes of service of process, whom must a nonresident applicant designate as their agent?
choice_a: The real estate commissioner
choice_b: Their affiliated broker's personal attorney
choice_c: The clerk of their home state's licensing board
choice_d: No agent designation is required of nonresidents
explanation: A nonresident applicant must designate the real estate commissioner as their agent for purposes of service of process arising out of any transaction involving Georgia real estate business.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(d), what discretion does the Commission have regarding other states' licensing authorities?
choice_a: It may enter written reciprocity agreements to assure Georgia licensees nonresident opportunities comparable to those the other state affords
choice_b: It must automatically grant reciprocity to every state without any agreement
choice_c: It is legally barred from entering any agreement with another state
choice_d: It may only negotiate agreements with states bordering Georgia
explanation: The Commission may, in its discretion, enter written agreements with similar licensing authorities in other states to secure comparable nonresident licensure opportunities for Georgia licensees.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(e), may a Georgia broker enter into a written agreement with an out-of-state broker who is not licensed in Georgia to conduct real estate business here?
choice_a: Yes, provided the agreement meets the statute's enumerated requirements and the out-of-state broker need not obtain a Georgia license
choice_b: No, every broker conducting any Georgia business must independently hold a Georgia license
choice_c: Only if the out-of-state broker relocates to Georgia within 90 days
choice_d: Only with the personal written approval of the Governor
explanation: O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(e) permits a Georgia broker to contract in writing with a licensed out-of-state broker to conduct Georgia real estate business without the out-of-state broker obtaining a Georgia license, provided the agreement satisfies the statute's requirements.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(e), who bears responsibility for real estate brokerage acts performed by an out-of-state broker under such a written agreement?
choice_a: The Georgia broker
choice_b: No one; the acts fall entirely outside Georgia's regulatory reach
choice_c: The out-of-state broker's home-state regulator has exclusive jurisdiction and Georgia has none
choice_d: The client alone bears the risk
explanation: Under such an agreement, the Georgia broker is responsible for all real estate brokerage acts performed by the out-of-state broker in connection with Georgia property.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(e), through whose trust account must trust funds be handled in a transaction involving a Georgia broker and an unlicensed out-of-state broker under such an agreement?
choice_a: The Georgia broker's trust account
choice_b: The out-of-state broker's home-state trust account exclusively
choice_c: A jointly-titled account requiring both brokers' signatures for every transaction
choice_d: No trust account is required in these arrangements
explanation: Under the required written agreement, trust funds from the transaction must be handled through the Georgia broker's trust or escrow account.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(e), what must contracts and advertisements arising from a Georgia broker/out-of-state broker agreement clearly do?
choice_a: Identify the Georgia broker and note that the out-of-state broker does not hold a Georgia real estate license
choice_b: Omit any reference to either broker to protect client privacy
choice_c: List only the out-of-state broker's name and license number
choice_d: Use a single combined business name that merges both brokers' identities
explanation: Contracts and advertisements must clearly identify the Georgia broker and give notice that the out-of-state broker is not licensed in Georgia.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-9(f), if an out-of-state broker under such an agreement violates Georgia law, to what is the Commission's enforcement authority generally limited?
choice_a: Suspending or revoking the Georgia broker's right to enter into such written agreements, unless the Georgia broker participated in or ratified the violation
choice_b: Imposing unlimited fines directly against the out-of-state broker's personal assets
choice_c: Extraditing the out-of-state broker to Georgia for criminal trial
choice_d: Automatically revoking the licenses of every affiliated licensee at the Georgia firm
explanation: Because the out-of-state broker is not Georgia-licensed, the Commission's enforcement authority for that broker's violations is generally limited to suspending or revoking the Georgia broker's right to enter such agreements, unless the Georgia broker participated in or ratified the violation.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-19(b), when an affiliated licensee leaves a broker, what must that broker do with the licensee's license?
choice_a: Immediately forward it to either the Commission or the licensee's new broker
choice_b: Destroy it to prevent unauthorized use
choice_c: Hold it indefinitely until the former licensee personally requests its return
choice_d: Mail it to the licensee's home address with no other option
explanation: Upon a licensee's departure, the broker must immediately forward the license to either the Commission or the licensee's new broker.

question: Under O.C.G.A. 43-40-19(b), when may a departing licensee resume real estate activities with a new broker?
choice_a: Only after personally delivering an approved transfer application to the Commission, or receiving a new wall certificate
choice_b: Immediately upon verbally notifying the new broker
choice_c: Only after a 90-day waiting period regardless of paperwork status
choice_d: As soon as the former broker verbally releases the licensee
explanation: A departing licensee cannot resume real estate activities under the new broker until either personally delivering an approved transfer application to the Commission or receiving a new wall certificate.

question: Per O.C.G.A. 43-40-19(d), absent the pre-transfer exception for enumerated transactions, for how many brokers may a salesperson or community association manager act as a licensee at one time?
choice_a: Only the one broker holding that salesperson's or CAM's license
choice_b: Up to three different brokers simultaneously
choice_c: Any broker who requests the licensee's assistance
choice_d: Any number, provided each pays a separate referral fee
explanation: A salesperson or community association manager may not act as a licensee for any broker other than the one holding that salesperson's or CAM's license, except as provided under the limited pre-transfer transaction exception.

question: Per Rule 520-4-.02, when does computation of a time period referred to in the Commission's procedural rules begin?
choice_a: With the first day following the day on which the act initiating the period occurs
choice_b: On the same calendar day the initiating act occurs
choice_c: On the first business day of the following month
choice_d: Only once the licensee formally acknowledges receipt
explanation: Under Rule 520-4-.02, computation of a time period begins with the first day following the day on which the act that initiates the period occurs, not the day of the act itself.

question: Under Rule 520-4-.02, if the last day of a computed time period falls on a day the Commission office is closed, what happens?
choice_a: The period runs until the end of the following business day
choice_b: The deadline is deemed to have already passed
choice_c: The period is shortened by the number of closed days
choice_d: The filer must submit the item electronically that same closed day
explanation: When the last day of a computed period falls on a day the Commission office is closed, the period runs until the end of the following business day.
